{"id": "36:69/q10", "question": "What can be inferred from the Prophet's encounters with poetic lines?", "turns_on": "The reported line, attribution, meter, correction, and chain differ across transmissions.", "positions": [{"id": "36:69/q10/p1", "position": "He sometimes quoted existing poetry with words or meter altered, then disclaimed being a poet.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha says it was his most disliked speech; al-Ḥasan’s Islam-and-gray-hair line and Ṭarafa’s unexpected-news line are recurring examples, with Abū Bakr or ʿUmar correcting him. Ibn Kathīr cites al-Tirmidhī’s ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ grading for a Ṭarafa report and al-Bukhārī’s correction of another wording."}, {"id": "36:69/q10/p2", "position": "He quoted or voiced correctly metered lines on rare occasions without becoming a poet.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī names a line of Ibn Rawāḥa; Ibn Kathīr notes authentic Trench work-song reports. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ preserve the fact of quotation alongside the denial of poetic authorship."}, {"id": "36:69/q10/p3", "position": "The poet behind the attempted line was al-Aʿshā.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā prefers this identification."}, {"id": "36:69/q10/p4", "position": "The poet behind the attempted line was Ṭarafa.", "reasons": "Several ʿĀʾisha versions and the report of an invocation against Ṭarafa name him; he corrected the words but called the meanings equivalent. Other versions call the poet a man of Banū Qays."}, {"id": "36:69/q10/p5", "position": "The quoted line was by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī attributes a line about unexpected news to him; Ibn Kathīr cites Trench work-songs; Abū Ḥayyān says its meter need not imply poetic craft."}, {"id": "36:69/q10/p6", "position": "The al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās spoil-division line was quoted with names reversed or reordered.", "reasons": "Ibn Hishām records the poem, a variant line, and the figurative 'cut his tongue' payment; Abū Bakr or al-ʿAbbās corrects al-Aqraʿ and ʿUyayna, with the Prophet saying the sense is the same. Al-Suhaylī sees the new order as honoring loyal al-Aqraʿ over later apostate ʿUyayna."}, {"id": "36:69/q10/p7", "position": "A report says he completed or composed one hopeful poetic line.", "reasons": "Al-Mizzī objects that its transmitters are unknown; al-Durr says the chain has an unknown narrator and ʿĀʾisha proposed a nonscanning inflection. Al-Ālūsī also marks an unknown narrator."}, {"id": "36:69/q10/p8", "position": "He began a line among the Badr dead and Abū Bakr completed it.", "reasons": "Al-Umāwī’s report is cited by Ibn Kathīr."}, {"id": "36:69/q10/p9", "position": "He identified a most poetic speaker by quoting a line beginning 'Do you not see me ... at night?'", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ālūsī give the question; Abū Ḥayyān includes this and the booty line."}, {"id": "36:69/q10/p10", "position": "He said he did not care if he used an antidote, wore an amulet, or composed poetry.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says Abū Dāwūd alone has the report; al-Durr also records it."}, {"id": "36:69/q10/p11", "position": "A rare report condemns composing a line after night prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr specifies composing, not merely reciting."}]}
{"id": "36:69/q11", "question": "Do accidentally metered Qur’anic or Prophetic phrases count as poetry?", "turns_on": "Whether poetry requires intent, minimum length, or a particular audible scansion.", "positions": [{"id": "36:69/q11/p1", "position": "No: poetry requires deliberate meter or poetic craft; natural speech may scan by accident.", "reasons": "Examples include 3:92, 18:29, 34:13, 61:13; the Prophet’s Ḥunayn 'I am the Prophet' and injured-finger sayings, and ordinary market speech. Al-Qurṭubī says the exact pronunciation is unknown; al-Nāsafī gives possible inflections, while the bloodied-finger line scans only with a particular tāʾ vowel."}, {"id": "36:69/q11/p2", "position": "The Ḥunayn line should be acknowledged as poetry or deliberate verse, making rejection of the report easier.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ finds denials of its meter or deliberateness less persuasive than rejecting the report."}, {"id": "36:69/q11/p3", "position": "A short rhymed line or two alone does not make a poet.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī is cited for a two-line minimum, and some require consistent meter or rhyme; al-Qurṭubī says even conceding poetry, rare quotation cannot make him learned in it."}, {"id": "36:69/q11/p4", "position": "Its poetic status depends on actual pronunciation and inflection.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī report claims that nominative or genitive endings break the 'I am the Prophet' meter; Ibn al-ʿArabī suggests those endings, but al-Qurṭubī notes pronunciation is not known. For the finger line, a kasra gives sarīʿ while a still tāʾ may not."}]}
{"id": "36:69/q12", "question": "How did the Prophet regard poetry as speech?", "turns_on": "Whether reports speak of all poetry or distinguish its content and amount.", "positions": [{"id": "36:69/q12/p1", "position": "He disliked poetry, especially excess or false, obscene, and satirical verse.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha repeats that it was his most disliked speech; Abū Hurayra's pus report is given with a strong chain by Ibn Kathīr, and al-Ālūsī construes it as excess. Bursavī distinguishes objectionable kinds."}, {"id": "36:69/q12/p2", "position": "He valued wise and morally useful poetry and supported Muslim poets.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl says some poetry was dear to him; he encouraged a Companion through 100 lines by Umayya, praised wisdom in poetry, and promised Ḥassān support by the Holy Spirit and a mosque pulpit. Al-Ālūsī reconciles these reports by kinds of verse."}, {"id": "36:69/q12/p3", "position": "A poet's wise words may coexist with a disbelieving heart.", "reasons": "The Prophet said Umayya’s poetry believed while his heart did not, according to Ibn Kathīr."}]}
{"id": "36:69/q13", "question": "What do the first denials imply about the final positive clause?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:69/q13/p1", "position": "The exclusive positive statement strengthens the denial: it is revelation, reminder and Qur’an, not poetry.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī compares 53:3–4; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ calls the restriction qaṣr al-qalb. {"id": "36:69/q14", "question": "What does the pronoun 'it' refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the antecedent is the delivered Qur’an, the Messenger, or the act of teaching.", "positions": [{"id": "36:69/q14/p1", "position": "The Qur’an or what was taught and delivered.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Nāsafī and al-Qurṭubī identify the revelation, which is clarified by the following nouns."}, {"id": "36:69/q14/p2", "position": "Muhammad himself is the reminder sent to people.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī explicitly identifies Muhammad as dhikr and the associated message as Qur’an; Qatāda instead identifies the phrase with this Qur’an."}, {"id": "36:69/q14/p3", "position": "The knowledge implied by 'We taught him'.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says the earlier verb supplies knowledge as an antecedent."}]}
{"id": "36:69/q15", "question": "What is dhikr here?", "turns_on": "Whether dhikr names the message or the Messenger.", "positions": [{"id": "36:69/q15/p1", "position": "A reminder, reflection, and admonition from God for people and jinn.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā includes believers among jinn and humans; al-Ḥasan says it recalls Paradise, while another report says it concerns God. Sahl stresses understanding and obedience. Iṣlāḥī says it recalls innate truths, the history of guidance and consequences of rejecting messengers; Study Quran notes earlier scriptures also called Reminder."}, {"id": "36:69/q15/p2", "position": "The Messenger Muhammad is himself the reminder sent to people.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī makes this identification, alongside the Qur’an as the message."}]}
{"id": "36:69/q16", "question": "What is meant by 'a clear Qur’an'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:69/q16/p1", "position": "A manifest divine recitation or book that clarifies truth and supplies guidance, duties and rulings.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās lists obligations, penalties and rulings; al-Ṭabrisī adds proofs and earlier nations. {"id": "36:69/q17", "question": "How is Qurʾān read and derived here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:69/q17/p1", "position": "A hamza-less qurān is linked to q-r-y, 'to gather', rather than q-r-ʾ, 'to read'.", "reasons": "The reading source says the emphasis shifts toward compilation."}]}
{"id": "36:69/q18", "question": "What does 'and' contribute between reminder and Qur’an?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:69/q18/p1", "position": "It joins distinct benefits of admonition and a recited comprehensive book.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says the labels are not redundant; Bursavī says the Qur’an includes rulings beyond admonition. {"id": "36:69/q20", "question": "What is the inward reading of not teaching poetry?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:69/q20/p1", "position": "God did not address Muhammad in coded, ambiguous speech or leave him ignorant of hidden intended meanings.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿArabī treats poetry as riddling and double meaning; Bursavī asks how this treats disconnected opening letters and suggests he may not see them as reserved ambiguity."}, {"id": "36:69/q20/p2", "position": "All skills and states ultimately come from divine teaching, through humans or directly.", "reasons": "Al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya cites 2:31 and David’s armor in 21:80; Bursavī adds craft by insight, Mathnawī lines on revelation and reason, and Cain learning burial from the crow in 5:31."}]}
{"id": "36:69/q21", "question": "Does the verse's denial extend to other prophets?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse's pronoun and rationale establish a general rule or a particular honor.", "positions": [{"id": "36:69/q21/p1", "position": "All prophets were barred from poetry.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports that the verse gives no apparent reason to restrict the denial to Muhammad."}, {"id": "36:69/q21/p2", "position": "Muhammad alone lacked poetic ability as an added honor; others may have ability without composing.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports a possibly authentic account of Adam composing verses after his son's death as support."}]}
{"id": "36:69/q22", "question": "What do unrelated grammatical examples in the collected notes establish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:69/q22/p1", "position": "Diminutives normally do not restore deleted roots, though reported irregular forms occur.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives miyyit and huwayr; Yūnus reports huwayʾir and Abū ʿAmr’s hamzated forms; the rule also controls other diminutives, with irregular forms not generalized."}, {"id": "36:69/q22/p2", "position": "Four- and five-radical words preserve original consonants; defective roots follow specific lengthening and weak-letter changes.", "reasons": "Sībawayh distinguishes jaʿfar and safarjal, rejects false augment analyses, and gives qawwal, buwiʿ, changed wāw/yāʾ, heavy hypothetical yawm forms, hamzated plurals and long-vowel patterns."}, {"id": "36:69/q22/p3", "position": "Nisba from two-radical nouns restores a lost final radical, with reported dialect and analogy exceptions.", "reasons": "Sībawayh cites abawī, akhawī, ḥamawī; al-Khalīl supports akhawī and calls Yūnus’s ukhtī nonanalogical.
